title: Quantitative analysis of polystyrene microplastic and styrene monomer released from plastic food containers
authors: Jiae Wang, Jieun Lee, Eilhann E. Kwon, Sanghyun Jeong
description: A laboratory experiment measured polystyrene particles released from an instant-noodle container under controlled pH, temperature, and contact-time conditions.
scope: Direct release experiment on PS instant-noodle container
findings:
A laboratory experiment measured polystyrene particles released from an instant-noodle container under controlled pH, temperature, and contact-time conditions.

Scroll the table horizontally to see source locations.

Test conditionReported resultParticle size contextSource location
200 mL pH 9 aqueous solution; maintained at 100 °C for 6 h{{claim:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers-ps-36}}Reported comparison bins: 10-100, 100-200, 200-300, >300 µm; predominantly 10-100 µmPDF p. 3 §2.2; p. 4 §2.3.2; p. 6 Figure 3(a); p. 7 §3.1
methods: Microscopy with FTIR chemical mapping identified particles on the filter. Styrene measured by GC-MS is a separate chemical result. Procedure blanks were reported to contain no microplastics.
fitness: Supports material-specific release under the stated laboratory conditions. It does not establish a release rate for reusable household tubs or a human health effect.
limitations: One commercial container type, not generic reusable tubs. pH 9 at 100 °C for 6 h is an extreme experiment. Figure 3(c) at 8 h exceeds the 36 at 6 h; 36 must not be described as the experiment-wide maximum. Supplementary size-distribution figure not supplied. 0.2 µm filtration pore is not a validated submicron detection floor. No estimate of ingested dose or human health effect.

methods: Nile Red fluorescence screened for particles. The workflow did not individually confirm each particle with FTIR or Raman. The particle table is separate from the HPLC monomer measurements. A cutting control is described, but its supplementary image was not reviewed.
fitness: Supports preliminary, method-specific particle observations from the tested packaging. Its counts should not be pooled with chemically confirmed particle counts, and its size examples are not full size distributions.
limitations: Cut pieces, not whole containers. Table 5 gives paired size examples and per-cm² piece ranges; it does not establish a sample-wide minimum/maximum size distribution, CI, or dose. Main article focuses on styrene, whose µg/mL values are not microplastic counts.

title: Simulation and Characterization of Nanoplastic Dissolution under Different Food Consumption Scenarios
authors: Ying Wang, Zhongtang Wang, Xin Lu, Hongyan Zhang, Zhenzhen Jia
description: The authors examined nanoplastic-sized material from a polypropylene takeaway box and composite heat-sealing packaging films under hot-water scenarios.
scope: Nanoplastic characterization under packaging scenarios, including PP box and heat-sealing film
findings:
The authors examined nanoplastic-sized material from a polypropylene takeaway box and composite heat-sealing packaging films under hot-water scenarios.

The polypropylene box and composite films were characterized separately. No particle count or concentration from this study is included in the Index. The heat-sealing films are not consumer zip-top storage bags.
methods: Sequential filtration, electron microscopy, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, and laser particle sizing characterized fractions after intensive sample preparation. Water controls were examined. Aggregation and subsequent ultrasound affect interpretation of particle size.
fitness: Supports qualitative material characterization under the studied scenarios. It supplies no accepted release concentration for this page and does not represent consumer zip-top bags.
limitations: PP box: 500 mL water at 100 °C for 20 min. GCPP/MCPP composite packaging: 121 °C for 20 min. Intensive detergent, acid, base and prolonged rinse pretreatment differs from ordinary consumer handling. Nominal filter fractions do not mean all dispersed objects stay in those size ranges; aggregates measured above range. Figure 5b label 167 versus text 168 for GCPP is inconsistent. No release concentration or count denominator suitable for public count summary. Do not generalize MCPP non-detection as safety or all bags as zip bags.

title: Detecting Micro- and Nanoplastics Released from Food Packaging: Challenges and Analytical Strategies
authors: Claudia Cella, Rita La Spina, Dora Mehn, Francesco Fumagalli, Giacomo Ceccone, Andrea Valsesia, Douglas Gilliland
description: Original experiments on polyethylene cooking and ice-cube bags, together with nylon tea bags, illustrate the challenges of identifying and quantifying material released from food packaging.
scope: Original experimental article on PE rice cooking bags, ice-cube bags and nylon teabags, not a methods review
findings:
Original experiments on polyethylene cooking and ice-cube bags, together with nylon tea bags, illustrate the challenges of identifying and quantifying material released from food packaging.

Commercial PE ice-cube bag: Raman identified PE particles mixed with ultramarine blue pigment and separate pigment particles. Room-temperature bag-contact control showed few visible particles, mainly PE. PDF p. 3 §2.2; pp. 6-7 Figure 1A and discussion.

Commercial PE rice-cooking bag with rice removed before test: Raman identified PE along with residual rice material. Boiled-water blank showed no PE or rice particles. PE mass by KBr-pellet FTIR was below the method detection limit. PDF p. 3 §2.2; pp. 6-7 Figure 1B and discussion; p. 9 mass quantification discussion.

For the ice-cube-bag test, bags contained 300 mL ultrapure water and were frozen at -20 °C for 24 h. The ice was manually removed into glass and thawed at room temperature. For the rice-cooking-bag test, the rice was removed before the bag was boiled in 250 mL ultrapure water at 100 °C for 10 min. These conditions belong to the studied bags and do not describe consumer zip-top storage bags. Source: PDF p. 3, section 2.2; pp. 6-7, Figure 1 and discussion.
methods: Raman microscopy identified polymer material; electron microscopy and XPS supplied complementary characterization. Calibrated FTIR assessed polymer mass. The study discusses laboratory blanks, unheated controls, and effects of sample concentration and preparation.
fitness: Supports qualitative findings for the specified cooking and ice-cube bags and explains measurement limitations. It does not supply a numerical particle-release rate used here, and the studied bags are not household zip-top storage bags.
limitations: Particle appearance and number depend on concentration, deposition, drying, cooling and aggregation. Polymer mass cannot be automatically converted to a particle count. Authors explicitly warn simple spotting is insufficient to quantify released particle number. Original sources studied are not zip-top storage bags.  No numerical particle release rate for the bag experiments is used here.

title: Microplastics and Nanoplastics in Foods
description: FDA explains its approach to microplastics in food and the limits of current analytical evidence.
findings: FDA states that food-contact materials require authorization for their intended uses and that the agency evaluates migration and toxicology data. It identifies unresolved analytical challenges and does not describe a standardized particle-count method for food.
methods: Official agency information, including the Regulatory Information and Scientific Information sections, accessed October 22, 2026. This is regulatory and scientific context, not a laboratory release experiment.
fitness: Supports statements about the FDA position described on the linked page.
limitations: It is not a product-specific compliance determination and does not set a release rate for a storage material.

title: Microplastics and nanoplastics in food
description: EFSA describes its scientific assessment role and remaining uncertainties for microplastics in food.
findings: EFSA describes evidence that particles can migrate from food-contact materials, alongside substantial data gaps and concerns about overestimation in some studies. Its topic page states that a full food risk assessment has not yet been completed.
methods: Official topic page, including Milestones, EFSA’s role, and FAQ, last reviewed October 21, 2026; accessed October 22, 2026.
fitness: Supports the stated scientific context and distinguishes EFSA assessment from legal limit-setting.
limitations: This topic page is not a legal instrument or a packaging compliance certificate.
